## Summary

We present a unified repertoire of indel mutational signatures in
6,975 tumors across 36 cancer types. Small insertions and deletions
("indels") are an important under-studied class of mutations. Koh,
Nanda, and colleagues recently introduced two richer indel
classifications, with 89 and 476 indel types. We identified signatures
separately in the two new classification schemes and the widely used
83-type classification scheme using two algorithms. We identified 44
89-type signatures and their 476-type counterparts; 26 are new.
Because lossless translation between the 83-type and newer schemes is
impossible, we used tumors dominated by single signatures to
exhaustively map correspondences across classifications. The 89- and,
especially, the 476-type schemes distinguish signatures and spectra
that the 83-type scheme cannot. We release software for generating and
plotting spectra in the new classifications. An accompanying web site
enables exploration of signatures and their cross-classification
relationships and provides a service to construct spectra from VCF
files.

## Graphical Abstract

## Highlights

1.  Repertoire of indel signatures across 6,975 genomes in 3 indel classification schemes

2.  Identified 26 novel 89-type and 11 novel 83-type classification indel signatures

3.  Integrative topography across transcription, replication, and genic regions

4.  Website and software for signature browsing and matrix generation from VCF files

# Introduction

Somatic mutations are caused by various mutational processes and
represent a driving force behind tumorigenesis and cancer development
[@alexandrovSignaturesMutationalProcesses2014]. These mutations can
result from either endogenous sources, such as 5-methylcytosine
deamination or defective DNA repair mechanisms
[@daviesHRDetectPredictorBRCA12017;
@cooperMethylationmediatedDeamination5methylcytosine2010;
@grollemanMutationalSignatureAnalysis2019;
@bootRecurrentMutationsTopoisomerase2022], or exogenous sources,
including exposure to chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke or certain
herbal medicines [@alexandrovMutationalSignaturesAssociated2016;
@ngAristolochicAcidsTheir2017;
@dziubanska-kusibabColibactinDNAdamageSignature2020;
@bootCharacterizationColibactinassociatedMutational2020]. Mutational
signature analysis provides insights into cancer etiology, prognosis,
prevention, [and evolution. Mutational]{.pink} signatures can also serve as biomarkers for mutagenic exposures.

By “mutational signatures” we mean distinctive patterns of mutations
left on genomes by mutagenic processes or exposures. They can be
identified by exposing cultured cells, organoids, or experimental
animals to suspected mutagens or perturbing DNA repair pathways and
then sequencing the affected genomes
[@bootIndepthCharacterizationCisplatin2018;
@huangGenomescaleMutationalSignatures2017;
@kucabCompendiumMutationalSignatures2019;
@caipagarciaTissueOrganoidCultures2024;
@rivaMutationalSignatureProfile2020]. In addition, machine learning
can identify mutational signatures as latent factors that explain the
patterns of mutations in large collections of somatic mutation data
[@alexandrovRepertoireMutationalSignatures2020;
@alexandrovSignaturesMutationalProcesses2014;
@nik-zainalMutationalProcessesMolding2012;
@chenDeepWholegenomeAnalysis2024; @kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025;
@degasperiSubstitutionMutationalSignatures2022;
@jinAccurateSensitiveMutational2024]. For example, data mining of
upper tract urothelial cancers (UTUC) from Taiwan initially identified
the aristolochic acid (AA) single-base substitution (SBS) signature
[@hoangMutationalSignatureAristolochic2013;
@poonGenomeWideMutationalSignatures2013]. Subsequent analysis revealed
that this signature was also present in bladder, kidney, and liver
cancers [@ngAristolochicAcidsTheir2017;
@poonMutationSignaturesImplicate2015]. More recently, data mining of
Chinese liver cancer genomes and experiments in cell culture showed
that AA also generates double-base-substitution (DBS) signatures and,
relevant to the current study, small insertion-and-deletion (indel)
signatures (Figure [-@fig-aa]) [@chenDeepWholegenomeAnalysis2024].

Mutational signature research [has focused less on indel than on SBS signatures. Symptomatic of this, COSMIC v3.6 catalogs only]{.pink}
25 indel signatures compared to 78 SBS signatures. Nevertheless, indel
signatures can yield important information for cancer classification,
epidemiology, and treatment and for understanding DNA repair and
mutagenic mechanisms. Examples include identification of tumors with
homologous recombination deficiency or with mismatch repair deficiency
[@huangMSIseqSoftwareAssessing2015; @kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025;
@daviesHRDetectPredictorBRCA12017] and a rare indel hypermutator
phenotype due to a mutation in topoisomerase 2 alpha
[@bootRecurrentMutationsTopoisomerase2022].

The first widely used classification of indels recognized 83 indel
types [@alexandrovRepertoireMutationalSignatures2020]. Recently,
@kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025 proposed two classification schemes,
one with 89 types of indel and one with 476 types (Figure [-@fig-aa]). [The 89-type scheme mainly consolidates similar mutation types in the 476-type classification into coarser-grained types (Table S1).]{.pink} [@kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025 derived 37 indel signatures in the 89-type classification from 4,775 genomes across seven cancer types, and showed that the finer resolution of 1 bp T insertions and deletions enables more nuanced exploration of the consequences of MMR defects. However, challenges remain in connecting the nomenclature of the 89-type signatures to the established 83-type system and in translating between the classification schemes.]{.pink}

The older, 83-type scheme primarily categorizes indels based on the
number of bases inserted or deleted, and for single-base insertions
and deletions the identity of the deleted or inserted base
(conventionally shown as pyrimidines, C or T). For these single-base
indels, the classification also considers the number of flanking C or
T residues (Figure [-@fig-aa]A). Indels longer than 1 base are further
classified by their occurrence within repetitive sequences (i.e.
microsatellites, simple tandem repeats). For deletions of ≥2 bases the
83-type system classification also encodes the presence of
microhomology. [(Microhomology is a hallmark of error-prone repair by non-homologous end-joining, notably in BRCA-deficient tumors.)]{.pink} For example, the 3-base deletion
(A**CA**\|T**CA**\|GG→A**CA**GG) exhibits a 2-base microhomology (CA).

[A prominent distinction is that, unlike the 83-type classification scheme, both new classifications distinguish]{.pink}
different types of indels of a single T or C according to the non-T
(respectively, non-C) flanking bases. This [substantially]{.yellow} improves
discrimination between mutational spectra and signatures containing
single-base indels, which are present in most signatures.

For example, the 83-type classification distinguishes deletions of
single Ts only by the number of T’s at the site of the deletion: 1, 2,
3, 4, 5, or ≥ 6 Ts (Figure [-@fig-aa]A). By contrast, the 89-type
classification distinguishes among deletions of T according to bases
preceding or following the sequence of Ts at the site of the deletion.
However, it groups together deletions of T from sequences of 1, 2, 3,
or 4 T, and groups together deletions of sequences of 5, 6, 7, 8, or more
Ts. Thus, for example, deletions of ATA→AA or ATTA→ATA are
distinguished from deletions of CTA→CA or CTTA→CTA, but the deletions
CTA→CA and CTTTTA→CTTTA have the same classification. The 476-type
classification scheme provides fine-grained distinctions among
deletions of a single C or T that combine the distinctions in the 83
and 89-type system. The 476-type classification scheme shows, for
example, that in the signature in Figure [-@fig-aa] (InsDel23), the
most prominent deletions are ATA→AA, CTA→CA, and GTA→GA. The
classifications of indels of 2 or more bases are less intuitive. Table
S1 provides a mapping from the 476-type classification to the 89 and
83-type classifications, as well as multiple examples of each category
of deletion.

Here, we analyzed somatic indels in 6,975 whole genomes to create a
comprehensive collection of indel signatures in all three
classification schemes using approaches based on hierarchical
Dirichlet processes and on non-negative matrix factorization. We
systematically matched the 476-type signatures to 89-type signatures
by collapsing the 476-type signatures to 89-type signatures and
comparing the collapsed signatures to signatures identified in the
89-type classification. We used tumor samples with spectra dominated
by single signatures to map signatures in the 83-type classification
to signatures in the other two classifications. We further profiled [signatures’ replication timing, transcription strand asymmetry, replication strand asymmetry, and asymmetry between genic and intergenic regions]{.pink}, providing insights into mutational processes underlying the
signatures. We also [tallied their associations with SBS signatures and with sex]{.pink}
within individual cancer types. Finally, in addition to the
supplementary information provided here, we also provide a web site to
facilitate exploration of these signatures (https://indelsig.net)[.]{.pink}

# Results

## Repertoire of indel signatures based on de novo signature discovery

We identified indel signatures in all three classifications from a
total of 6,975 cancer genomes encompassing 36 cancer types using a
method based on hierarchical Dirichlet processes
[@liuMSigHdpHierarchicalDirichlet2023], and a method based on
non-negative matrix factorization
[@islamUncoveringNovelMutational2022]. The extracted signatures were
broadly consistent between the two methods (Table [-@tbl-corr], Tables
S2-S8). We identified 44 mutational signatures in the new 89-type
classification and, independently, the 44 corresponding signatures in the [476-type]{.pink} classification. We assessed concordance between
signatures identified in two classification systems by collapsing the
476-type signatures to their 89-type counterparts and comparing them
to signatures extracted in the 89-type classification. Mean cosine
similarity was \> 0.989 (median \> 0.994, minimum \> 0.951), [providing
evidence that these signatures constitute latent factors robust to the
feature set in which they were discovered]{.blue}. Further evidence of their
robustness derives from the identification of tumor spectra dominated
by a single signature. For 35 of the 44 signatures, there were tumor spectra with cosine similarity \> 0.95[,]{.pink} and for 39
there were tumor spectra with similarity \> 0.90 (Table [-@tbl-corr]).
[Of the 44 89-type signatures, 18 were similar (cosine similarity ≥ 0.85, see Methods) to signatures described by @kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025, and 26 were, to our knowledge, not previously described (Table [-@tbl-corr]). Of the 34 signatures we discovered in the 83-type classification, 20 were similar to COSMIC reference signatures, 3 were similar to signatures described by @jinAccurateSensitiveMutational2024, and 11 were not previously described (Table [-@tbl-corr]).]{.pink}

::: {.callout-note title="Reviewer note"}
[Problem: High cosine similarity between collapsed 476-type and 89-type signatures shows the two extractions agree, not that the factors are robust to any feature set. Proposed: "indicating that signature discovery in the two classifications yielded consistent results".]{.blue}
:::

Because lossless translation between signatures in the 83-type and the
two new classification schemes is impossible (Table S1), we used tumor
mutational spectra dominated by individual signatures to
systematically elucidate signature correspondences across
classification schemes. Table [-@tbl-corr] shows the correspondences,
with details and discussion in https://indelsig.net/.

In several cases, the new indel classifications systems were able to
distinguish signatures that the older system merged. This is clearest
for deletions of single T bases from tracts of ≥ 6 Ts. Our data set
had \> 8.5 million of these deletions out of 18.4 million deletions in
total. The COSMIC reference signature ID2 in the older, 83-type
classification, consists exclusively of these deletions. The new indel
classifications divide ID2 into three signatures. Among these,
InsDel2b is dominated by deletions of T from tracts of 5 to 7 Ts.
InsDel2a and InsDel2c are both dominated by deletions of single Ts
from stretches of ≥ 8 Ts. However, they are distinguished by
InsDel2a’s preference for flanking A bases and InsDel2c’s preference
for flanking C bases. Mutations attributed to InsDel2b and InsDel2c
are strongly enriched among MSI-H tumors. Furthermore, the counts of
mutations attributed to these signatures are correlated with the
counts of mutations attributed to the MSI-H-associated SBS signatures
SBS6, SBS26, and SBS44 (Figure [-@fig-assoc], Figure S1).

[The same is true for insertions of single T bases into long poly-T tracts.]{.pink} Our data set had 3.3 million
insertions of single T bases into tracts of ≥ 5 Ts, which in the
83-type system constitutes a single mutation class, and COSMIC
reference signature ID1 consists exclusively of this class of
insertions. The new indel classifications divide ID1 into three
signatures. Among these, InsDel1a has the largest proportion of
insertions into tracts of ≥ 8 Ts and InsDel1b has the smallest
proportion, while InsDel1c has an intermediate proportion. Compared to
InsDel1b, InsDel1a and InsDel1c have larger proportions of A to the
left of the poly-T tract and G to the right, and smaller proportions
of C to the left of the poly-T tract with C or A to the right.
InsDel1b is further distinguished from InsDel1a and 1c in that several
tumors with high proportions of InsDel1b (\> 0.4) have mutations in
the proofreading domain of polymerase epsilon (Table S9).

***Two signatures in which the 89-type classification misses clear
differences***

While the 89-type classification system on the whole better
discriminates signatures, in two cases the 83-type and [476-type systems clearly differentiated signatures that were almost identical in the 89-type system]{.pink}. One case consisted of InsDel13 and InsDel_C.
These are nearly identical in the 89-type system, which groups
deletions of single Ts in stretches of 1, 2, 3, or 4 Ts as a single
deletion type. However[,]{.pink} the 83[-]{.pink} and [476-type]{.pink} systems show that InsDel_C
has deletions of 1 T from ATA (ATA→AA), while InsDel13 has deletions
of T from ATTA (ATTA→ATA, Figure S2A). The other case consisted of
InsDel11 and InsDel16. InsDel11 has insertions of one C next to an
isolated C (C with non-Cs on each side, e.g. ACG→ACCG) and insertion of [one]{.pink} T next to an isolated T (e.g. GTG→GTTG). InsDel16 has
insertion of one C between non-Cs (e.g. AT→ACT), and insertion of one
T between non-Ts (e.g. AG→ATG, Figure S2B). Again, the 89-type system
does not capture these differences, while the 83 and 476-type systems
do.

***Clarified signatures of aristolochic-acid-induced deletions***

InsDel23 is caused by aristolochic acid (AA) exposure and the 476-type [signature shows]{.pink} that most AA deletions involve 5’TA3’/3’AT5’ → A/T
(Figure [-@fig-aa], and see https://indelsig.net). This pattern is not
visible in either the 83-type or 89-type classification. 
One might speculate that this
pattern is related to the adenine adducts caused by AA, which are also
thought to be responsible for the predominance of A→T single base
substitutions in the AA SBS signature and for the frequent involvement
of adenines in the AA DBS signature.

***APOBEC3A activity and InsDel_Aβ***

We identified InsDel_Aβ, an indel signature that in the 476-type
classification consists primarily of 1 bp C deletions TCA→TA and [TCT→TT (Figure S2C, right sub-panel)]{.pink}. Thus, InsDel_Aβ
targets the same sequences as the canonical APOBEC SBS signatures SBS2
(TCA→TTA and TCT→TTT) and SBS13 (TCA→TGA and TCT→TGT). Experiments in
cell culture showed that, in addition to single nucleotide
substitutions, APOBEC3A induces indels, mainly TC→T
[@deweerdProspectivelyDefinedPatterns2022]. In parallel, we discovered
the corresponding 83-type indel signature, ID_A, which, compared to
C_ID9, is more similar to the experimental indel spectrum in
@deweerdProspectivelyDefinedPatterns2022. [Notably, ID9 and InsDel9 in all three classifications have many deletions of single thymines, while ID_A and InsDel_Aβ lack these]{.pink} (Figure S2C). In addition, the InsDel9
476-type signature also has many deletions of a single C following A
or G, while InsDel_Aβ has almost exclusively deletions of a single C
following T. This signature was also noted in
@kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025, who denoted it InD9a. We propose that
this signature is distinct enough from InsDel9 in the 476-type
classification to warrant an identifier.

***MSS tumors: single-thymine indels in poly-T tracts***

[De novo signature discovery using both HDP and NMF in all three]{.pink} indel
signature classifications identified signatures with similar
proportions of deletions and insertions of a single thymine in poly-T
tracts. These occur almost exclusively in MSS tumors. We termed these
ID_N (the 83-type signature) plus InsDel_Nα and InsDel_Nβ (the 89- and
476-type signatures). Previous analysis in the 83-type classification
allocated insertions and deletions of single thymines in poly-T tracts
to separate signatures ID1 and ID2, and did not differentiate between
signature occurrence in MSS versus MSI-H
[@alexandrovRepertoireMutationalSignatures2020]. We first focus on
InsDel_Nβ which occurs in 2,629 of 6,770 MSS tumors (39%) in diverse
cancer types and in only 9 of [175]{.pink} MSI-H tumors (5%, Table S10).
Roughly half the tumors with InsDel_Nβ also have InsDel1a, and
InsDel1a also occurs without InsDel_Nβ in 2,596 MSS tumors ([38%]{.pink}) and
35 MSI-H tumors (20%). Thus, many MSS tumors have roughly equal
proportions of thymine deletions and insertion in long poly-T tracts
(InsDel_Nβ[)]{.pink}, but other tumors have varying proportions of additional
insertions ([InsDel1a]{.pink}), and some tumor spectra are completely
dominated by these insertions. The other signature with approximately
equal proportions of insertions and deletions of a thymine in a poly-T
tract, InsDel_Nα, is rare in both MSS and MSI-H tumors, occurring in
only 55 of 6,770 MSS tumors and 2 of 175 MSI-H tumors.

***Indels in poly-T tracts and microsatellite contraction in MSI-H
tumors***

In addition to enrichment for InsDel2a, 2b, and 2c, which represent
single-thymine deletions from poly-T tracts, MSI-H tumors were notably
enriched for signatures [InsDel7, InsDel_D, and InsDel_J]{.pink} (Figure [-@fig-assoc][A]{.pink}).
InsDel7, like InsDel2a/b/c, is dominated by single-thymine deletions
from poly-T tracts, but with a distinct distribution of sequences
flanking the poly-T tract. InsDel_J consists almost entirely of
deletions of single dinucleotides from [dinucleotide microsatellites]{.pink},
e.g. deletion of CA from (CA)^5^, or deletion of GT from (GT)^8^ \[see
also entries for the 476-indel-type category Del2:U2:R(5,) in Table
S1\]. [Another signature, InsDel1a, which is dominated by single-thymine insertions into poly-T tracts, occurred without InsDel_Nβ in 20% of MSI-H tumors compared with 38% of MSS tumors (Table S10).]{.pink}

## The new indel classifications reveal an accurate signature of RNase H2 deficiency

Cells with RNase H2 deficiency cannot efficiently remove
ribonucleotides that had previously been incorporated into genomic
DNA, and this sets the stage for topoisomerase-1 (TOP1) associated
mutagenesis. This was previously proposed to generate indel signature
ID4 [@reijnsSignaturesTOP1Transcriptionassociated2022;
@kohRedefinedInDelTaxonomy2025; @jinAccurateSensitiveMutational2024].
[However, we detected a new indel signature, InsDel_F,]{.blue} which [corresponds better to experimental RNase H2 deficiency data than does ID4/InsDel4]{.pink} (Figure
[-@fig-rnaseh2], Figure S5). The profile of deletions of ≥2 bases is
very different between InsDel_F and [InsDel4]{.pink}: InsDel_F has distinctively
high proportions of (i) 2-base deletions with microhomology (almost
all TCT → T or TGT → T) and (ii) 2-base deletions from paired 2-base
doublets (most often CTCT → CT). InsDel4 has much lower proportions of
these two deletion types and also has additional prominent deletion
types that are essentially absent in InsDel_F. These additional
deletion types are mainly deletions of 3 or 4 bases with microhomology
and deletions of 3 or 4 bases from paired doublets (e.g. TCTTCT → TCT,
GTTTGTTT → GTTT). The spectra in RNase H2 deficient cell lines consist
of signatures due to mutational processes intrinsic to the parental
cell line combined with high proportions of mutations characteristic
of InsDel_F (Figure S5). Like InsDel_F, these cell-line spectra have
2-base deletions with microhomology and 2-base deletions from paired
2-base doublets. These spectra conspicuously lack the 3- and 4-base
deletions present in InsDel4. Similarly, RNase H2 deficient mouse
tumors have high proportions of the 2-base deletions characteristic of
InsDel_F and lack the 3 and 4 base deletions present in InsDel4.

### *Associations between indel signatures and SBS signatures*

We further analyzed the correlations between the indel signature
activities we derived and the SBS signature activities from
@degasperiSubstitutionMutationalSignatures2022 (Tables S11, S12). We
first computed a matrix of [correlations between the numbers of mutations attributed to each SBS signature and to each indel signature, for all SBS-indel signature pairs.]{.pink}
Agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the rows and columns of this
matrix using 1 – the Pearson correlation coefficient as distance
identified several clusters (Figure [-@fig-assoc]B). The
APOBEC-related cluster includes SBS2 and SBS13 and showed moderate
correlations with ID_A and InsDel_Aβ. The homologous recombination
deficiency [(HRD)]{.pink} cluster, consisting of SBS3 and SBS8, was strongly
associated with InsDel6 and InsDel9 (Figure [-@fig-assoc]B, “HR
defects”). UV-related signatures, such as SBS7a, SBS38, InsDel13, and
InsDel_H, also clustered together, [consistent with]{.yellow} their shared etiology.
The cluster related to mutations in the proofreading domain of the
polymerase epsilon (*POLE*) gene [linked SBS10a with InsDel1b and InsDel_K.]{.pink} [Additional
analysis of tumor somatic mutations confirmed that these signatures
are associated with dysfunctional *POLE* proofreading plus, in some
tumors, mismatch repair deficiency]{.blue} (Table S9 \<add hypermutator info
to legend\>).

::: {.callout-note title="Reviewer note"}
[Problem: "Confirmed" overstates a supplementary table. Proposed: "Tumors with high InsDel1b or InsDel_K activity frequently carried POLE proofreading domain mutations and, in some cases, mismatch repair deficiency".]{.blue}
:::

Within the mismatch repair deficiency (MMR) cluster, we observed a
strong network of correlations between SBS6, SBS26, SBS44, and a group
of indel signatures, including C_ID2, InsDel2b, InsDel2c, InsDel7,
InsDel_D, and InsDel_J (Figure [-@fig-assoc], “MMR defects”). Another
notable group included InsDel_B, InsDel5a, and InsDel5b, which
co-occurred with liver-cancer associated SBS signatures SBS12 and
SBS16.

The 89-type taxonomy also allowed us to better resolve the
relationships within previously broader categories. For instance, the
three signatures derived from C_ID1 (InsDel1a, InsDel1b, and InsDel1c)
each showed distinct patterns of correlation to SBS signatures (Figure
[-@fig-assoc]B). InsDel1a and the 83-type signature C_ID1 had similar
correlation profiles and frequently co-occurred with SBS88, SBS17, and
SBS93, which are prominent in the [gastrointestinal (GI) cluster]{.pink}. In contrast,
InsDel1b was linked to *POLE* proofreading errors and InsDel1c was
associated with SBS liver cancer signatures SBS12 and SBS16.

These correlation patterns provide insight into the possible origins
of previously uncharacterized SBS signatures. For example, SBS92
closely mirrored the correlation profile of SBS4, with strong
associations with C_ID3 and InsDel3b, further supporting a link with
tobacco smoking (Figure [-@fig-assoc]B, “Tobacco Smoking”)
[@lawsonExtensiveHeterogeneitySomatic2020]. In the [GI]{.pink} cluster, which includes signatures common in gastrointestinal
tumors (SBS17, SBS18, SBS1, SBS88, and SBS93), we observed that
C_ID18/InsDel18, ID_N/InsDel_Nβ were associated with SBS signatures
typically seen in the GI tract. 
[SBS93, which was previously found almost exclusively
in stomach and esophageal tumors with transcriptional strand bias suggesting thymine
damage [@islamUncoveringNovelMutational2022; @moodyMutationalSignaturesEsophageal2021],
was highly correlated with C_ID14/InsDel14.]{.blue} 
In addition C_ID1 and
InsDel1a had stronger correlations with SBS1 and SBS18, [supporting
their association with mutagenesis driven by reactive oxygen species]{.blue}
(Figure [-@fig-assoc]).

## Topography of indel mutational signatures \<STEVE REVIEW\>

We evaluated the interplay between [the 83-type signatures we identified]{.pink} and several genomic topographical features.
Transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair [is]{.pink} known to cause
transcription strand asymmetries, since DNA bulky adducts on the
transcribed strand will be preferentially repaired in the
transcription active region across the genome (add cite).
[Transcription strand asymmetries were shown in 17 out of 33 83-type
signatures]{.blue} (Figure [-@fig-topo]A, Figure S3A, Table S13). Signatures
attributed to exogenous mutational processes, such as C_ID3 (tobacco
smoking exposure), C_ID14 (correlated with SBS93) and C_ID18
(colibactin exposure), showed consistent transcription strand bias[, with mutations enriched on]{.pink} the transcribed strand. Another exogenous
mutational signature C_ID13, which is attributed to UV exposure,
showed enrichment [on]{.pink} the untranscribed strand. [This is because UV
damage occurs on cytosine rather than guanine.]{.blue} In
83-type signatures associated with defective endogenous mutational
processes, enriched mutations on the untranscribed strand were
observed for C_ID1 (slippage during DNA replication) and C_ID5
(clock-like signature), while enriched mutations on the transcribed
strand were observed for ID_F (topoisomerase-1 \[TOP1\] associated
mutagenesis stemming from RNase H2 deficiency). [Interestingly, 3
defective MMR signatures also showed transcription strand asymmetries
in different directions, with two of them (C_ID7 and ID_K) having
enriched mutations on the transcribed strand, and one of them (ID_N)]{.blue}
having enriched mutations mainly on the untranscribed strand.
Replication strand asymmetries were observed in 12 out of 33 83-type
signatures (Figure [-@fig-topo]B, Figure S3B, Table S13). Analogous to
transcription strand asymmetries, the majority of signatures
attributable to exogenous mutagenic exposures or defective endogenous
repair processes exhibited pronounced replication strand bias,
manifesting preferentially on either the leading or lagging strand.
ID_K, which [is enriched in tumors with POLE proofreading defects]{.yellow}, was consistently enriched for leading strand mutations. This
is consistent with SBS signatures SBS10a and SBS10b, which are also
driven by POLE proofreading defects, thus further supporting a
link between POLE proofreading defects and leading-strand mutagenesis.

# Discussion

In this study, we analyzed somatic indels in 6,975 whole-genome tumor
samples spanning 36 cancer types and established a comprehensive
repertoire of indel mutational signatures across the 83-type, 89-type,
and 476-type classification systems. By combining de novo signature
discovery with systematic cross-classification mapping, we show that
the 89-type and 476-type taxonomies provide substantially greater
resolution than the conventional 83-type scheme, particularly for
single-base insertions and deletions in context-dependent sequence
environments. This expanded framework not only clarifies
correspondences among previously reported signatures, but also enables
the identification of novel signatures, including ID_F and InsDel_F,
which are associated with TOP1-related mutagenesis and RNase H2
deficiency. [In addition, we identified six 89-type and 476-type
signatures, together with four 83-type signatures, that are strongly
enriched in high-mutation-burden tumors,]{.blue} and further refined the
interpretation of indel processes linked to mismatch repair deficiency
and/or POLE/POLD proofreading dysfunction. [By analyzing a larger and more diverse cancer genome cohort, we not only expanded the existing indel signature database, but also systematically linked and unified the nomenclature of the 83-type and 89-type signatures.]{.pink}

::: {.callout-note title="Reviewer note"}
[Problem: This result is not reported in the Results section. Proposed: Add the result to Results (with a figure or table reference) or drop the sentence.]{.blue}
:::



A major strength of this study is the systematic mapping between the
conventional 83-type scheme and the newer 89-type and 476-type indel
taxonomies. Because translation across these classification systems is
inherently imperfect, direct comparison of signatures is not
straightforward. By leveraging tumors dominated by single mutational
processes, [we established robust correspondences among signatures
identified in all three frameworks]{.blue}. This unified mapping not only
improves continuity with legacy studies based on the 83-type
classification, but also provides a practical reference structure that
will facilitate future indel signature analyses using the more
informative 89-type and 476-type schemes.

::: {.callout-note title="Reviewer note"}
[Problem: Table 1 has 9 of 44 signatures without a tumor at > 0.90 similarity and several matches required zeroing poly-T insertions. Proposed: "we established correspondences for most signatures across the three frameworks".]{.blue}
:::

The new indel framework also refined the interpretation of several
biologically important mutational processes. Notably, the new
TOP1-associated signatures, ID_F and InsDel_F, were more consistent
with RNase H2 deficiency than previously recognized indel patterns.
The enrichment of microhomology-mediated deletions and paired doublet
deletions in these signatures supports a mechanistic link between
RNase H2 dysfunction and a characteristic indel spectrum. Similarly,
we identified multiple signatures strongly associated with
microsatellite instability, and the finer resolution of the new
taxonomies allowed us to distinguish MSI-related signatures that were
previously aggregated or less clearly resolved. Given the clinical
relevance of MSI and mismatch repair deficiency, [this improved
annotation may have direct utility for tumor classification and
therapeutic stratification]{.blue}.

::: {.callout-note title="Reviewer note"}
[Problem: Nothing in the paper tests utility for classification or stratification. Proposed: "this improved annotation may be useful for tumor classification".]{.blue}
:::

Our integrative analyses also examined the relationships between indel
signatures and SBS signatures. The clustering of APOBEC-, UV-, HR-,
MMR-, and POLE-related signatures is consistent with shared or linked
mutational processes across mutation classes, supporting the idea that
indel mutational signatures often arise in the context of broader
mutational programs. These associations provide an additional layer of
biological interpretation and help connect indel signatures to
established mutagenic pathways.

We also investigated the genome-wide topographical features associated
with indel signatures, including transcriptional strand bias,
replication strand bias, genic distribution, and replication timing.
Notably, because the COSMIC catalog does not provide such
topographical annotations for many indel signatures, [our analysis in
this large cohort helps fill an important gap in the current knowledge
base]{.blue}. 
The observed associations highlight the influence of DNA repair
and replication dynamics on indel formation and suggest that genomic
context contributes to the emergence and distribution of distinct
indel patterns. Together, these analyses provide a more comprehensive
view of the biological determinants of indel mutagenesis.

Importantly, the 89-type system is not uniformly superior in all
settings. Although it improves resolution for indels occurring in long
poly-T tracts, it also compresses indels of length greater than or
equal to 2 bp, and in some cases may merge biologically distinct
patterns that are separated in the 83-type framework. For example, the
relationships between InsDel_C and InsDel13, as well as between
InsDel11 and InsDel16, suggest that some signatures with distinct
sequence preferences in the 83-type system are represented together in
the 89-type taxonomy.  Taken together, these results
suggest that although the 89-type taxonomy represents an important
advance, further refinement of indel classification will be needed to
fully capture the diversity of indel mutational processes. The unified
framework presented here should therefore support more consistent
interpretation of current signatures and provide a foundation for
future development of an even more informative indel taxonomy.

# Materials and methods

## Data sources

Somatic indel calls from the ICGC/TCGA (International Cancer Genome
Consortium/The Cancer Genome Atlas) Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole
Genomes Consortium and associated clinical characteristics were
obtained from the ICGC data portal
(<https://dcc.icgc.org/releases/current/Projects/>, which has been
retired. The data were downloaded on 9 May, 2024). Hartwig Medical
Foundation (Hartwig) through standardized procedures and request forms
that can be found at
https://www.hartwigmedicalfoundation.nl/en/appyling-for-data/.
Clinical traits such as cancer type, age and gender of the Hartwig
genomes were found from supplementary files of
@priestleyPancancerWholegenomeAnalyses2019. \<we can duplicate this in
the code but we don’t need to re-present the Priestly table\> These
data are also available in Table S16 in
@priestleyPancancerWholegenomeAnalyses2019.

## De novo Mutational signature extraction

*De novo* mutational signature extraction was performed using two
complementary tools applied to the 83-type, 89-type, and 476-type
mutational spectra. A stratified strategy was adopted to capture rare
and cancer-specific signatures, encompassing analyses of all genomes,
specific cancer types, high-TMB samples, and the PCAWG and Hartwig
cohorts individually.

For the hierarchical Dirichlet process–based approach, mSigHdp
(v2.1.2) was used. When analyzing all samples, cancer type was used to
define the hierarchical structure of the model. For analyses
restricted to individual cancer types or to genomes with high tumor
mutational burden, de novo signatures were extracted using two‑layer
hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) mixture models. In all mSigHdp
analyses, the following parameters were applied: seedNumber = 1234,
burnin = 1000, burnin.multiplier = 20, post.n = 200, post.space = 100,
num.child.process = 20, gamma.alpha = 1, and gamma.beta = 50. For
analyses including all samples or genomes with high tumor mutational
burden, an additional downsampling step was applied
(downsample_threshold = 3000) to reduce computational time.

In parallel, de novo mutational signatures were extracted using the
Non-negative matrix factorization based approach (NMF),
SigProfilerExtractor (v1.1.24). For analyses including all genomes,
NMF was performed with the number of signatures evaluated between 10
and 40 (minimum_signatures = 10; maximum_signatures = 40). For
analyses restricted to individual cancer types or to genomes with high
tumor mutational burden, the number of signatures evaluated ranged
from 2 to 20 (minimum_signatures = 2; maximum_signatures = 20). Each
factorization was repeated 100 times (nmf_replicates = 100), with all
other parameters set to their recommended default values. Most
signatures were extracted at the “Optimal Solution” identified by
SigProfilerExtractor, although several rare signatures were identified
in alternative solutions.

## Match 83-type and 89-type signatures into reference signatures

For 83-type signatures, the signatures were matched to previously
identified COSMIC signatures (v3.5,
<https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/signatures/id/>). For 89-type signatures,
the signatures supported by both mSigHdp and SigProfilerExtractor were
matched to the signatures reported in Koh et al. A detailed comparison
can be found in Table [-@tbl-corr].

We compared all *de novo* signatures supported by both mSigHdp and
SigProfilerExtractor to the published signatures and categorized them
into three groups: (1) known signature: if an extracted signature has
a cosine similarity of ≥ 0.85 with a COSMIC signature; (2) merged
signatures: if an extracted signatures can be reconstructed by at most
3 COSMIC signatures with a reconstructed similarity of ≥ 0.9; (3)
novel signatures: the extracted signatures do not fit into the known
signatures or the merged signatures. We focused on (1) and (3) in this
study.

## Assignment of signature activity to each individual genome

To leverage the resolution of both the 83-type and 89-type mutational
signatures, we constructed a unified 172-type reference set and
applied SigProfilerAssignment to decompose the 172-type spectra in
low-TMB tumors (indels \< 5,000). In contrast, high-TMB tumors (indels
≥ 5,000), as well as tumors where 1-bp T insertions or deletions in at
least five poly-T tracts account for ≥50% of the mutations (Table
S18), often exhibited highly sparse spectra. This sparsity further
masks other mutational signals. Therefore regarding these cases, we
employed mSigAct, estimating likelihoods under a multinomial
distribution. This was performed in a two-step computational
framework. First, we applied the find_best_reconstruction_QP function
from the mSigTools R package (v1.0.7), which performs fast signature
attribution via quadratic programming optimization. Second, we refined
these initial estimates using the PresenceAttributeSigActivity
function from the mSigAct R package. Final signature assignments were
obtained by integrating results from SigProfilerAssignment for low-TMB
tumors and mSigAct for high-TMB tumors.

## Simulating synthetic cancer datasets

We generated synthetic cancer datasets in 83-type indels using
SigProfilerSimulator
(<https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12859-020-03772-3>).

## Annotating somatic indels based on transcribed versus untranscribed strand

We followed the method in
(<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2023.112930>). Briefly, somatic
indels were called with respect to the + strand of the reference
genome and further annotated in regard to the pyrimidine base(s) of
the insertion/deletion. Thus, indels with only C or T bases were
annotated as + strand mutations; indels with only A or G bases were
annotated as – strand mutations. The remaining indels were not
included in the analysis. Next, + strand indels in protein coding
genes were further subclassified as transcribed (template) if the
gene’s sense strand was on the + strand of the genome, or else
untranscribed (sense). The logic was inverted for – strand indels.
Indels in bidirectionally transcribed regions were ignored.

## Annotating somatic indels based on leading versus lagging replication strand

Replication strand was determined by wavelet-smoothed
replication-timing signal data that indicated both “valleys”
(replication termination zones) and “peaks” (replication initiation
zones)
(<https://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg19/encodeDCC/wgEncodeUwRepliSeq/>).
Valleys and peaks were sorted by the genomic coordinate in ascending
order. In regard to + strand of the reference genome, replication
timing signals were examined for consecutive stretches of the genome
(from valley to peak or from peak to valley), with positive slope
corresponded to leading strand regions and negative slope corresponded
to lagging strand regions. Then for the - strand of the reference
genome, leading regions (- slope) and lagging regions (+slope) were
automatically acquired. Similar to the annotation for transcription,
indels were first annotated as + or – strand mutations based on the
pyrimidine bases. Next, indels were counted as being on leading strand
or lagging strand based on their occupancy in a leading or lagging
region.

## Detecting strand asymmetries across cancer types

Strand asymmetry analyses were based on the assignment of signature
probabilities to each individual indel mutation. Only indels with the
probability greater than or equal to 0.50 to a certain indel signature
were retained. For each indel signature and for all cancer types
having this mutational signature, we retrieved the number of indels on
each strand/region. In strand asymmetries analyses, only cancer types
with at least 1,000 somatic mutations unambiguously attributed to an
individual mutational signature were included.

For each strand asymmetry analyses (genic and intergenic region
asymmetry, transcription strand asymmetry, replication strand
asymmetry), indel mutations were split into two types and counted
(genic vs intergenic mutation, leading strand vs lagging strand
mutation, untranscribed strand vs transcribed strand mutation). The
two types were denoted as +/- strand mutations in all
three cases. The ratio of real somatic indels and the ratio of
simulated somatic indels was calculated separately:

strand ratio = (+ strand_mutation_counts)·(- strand_mutation_counts)^-1^

We calculated the odds ratio between the strand ratio of real somatic
indels and the strand ratio of simulated somatic indels.

We then calculated p values for the odds ratio using
Fisher’s exact test. Only strand asymmetries with p value \< 0.05 were
considered to show strand asymmetries.

For a given cancer type, for e.g. genic vs non-in a sup table

genic non-genic

real 100 600

syn 100 300

## Analyses of replication timing across cancer types

Replication timing data were obtained from
(<https://genomebiology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13059-018-1509-y>)
The replication time signals were sorted in a descending order and
subsequently divided into deciles. Somatic indels were counted within
the corresponding deciles based on their overlap with the replication
domains in the examined deciles. As with other analyses, for each
individual indel signature, the reported replication timing analyses
included only cancer types with at least 1,000 somatic mutations
unambiguously attributed to it.

Replication timing mutation counts were generated for both real and
simulated somatic indels. To classify whether the replication timing
mutation density was increasing, flat, or decreasing, two linear
regression models were fitted to the values of the real somatic indels
count *R* = (*R~1~, R~2~, R~3~, … R~10~*) and the values of simulated
somatic indel counts S(X~1~, X~2~, X~3~, … X~10~), respectively. The
two models are *lm(R \~ c )* and *lm(S \~ c)*, where replication
timing denotes a vector c = (1,2,3 … 10).

The replication timing trend for an 83-type signature was determined
for both real and simulated data. An indel signature was considered to
be generally unaffected by replication timing if the slope m was not
statistically significant from a flat line. Otherwise, with the slope
m statistically significant from a flat line, an ID signature was
considered to be increasing from early to late replicating regions if
the slope m \> 0, and was considered to be decreasing from early to
late replicating regions if the slope m \< 0.

If the trends of a certain 83-type signature for the two datasets
(real and simulated data) were different, the relative trend for real
data comparing the simulated data was the final trend for the 83-type
signature. Otherwise, if the trends of a certain 83-type signature for
the two dataset were the same, a third multiple linear regression
model was fitted: *lm(R \~ S + c)*

Similarly, the final trend of an 83-type signature were determined by
the significance of the coefficient of replication timing. If it is
not significant, an 83-type signature was considered to be generally
unaffected by replication timing. Otherwise, if the coefficient of
replication timing \> 0, an 83-type signature was considered to be
increasing from early to late replicating regions; if the coefficient
of replication timing \< 0, an 83-type signature was considered to be
decreasing from early to late replicating regions.

## MSI/MSS status and high/low TMB status

For PCAWG genomes, the MSI (microsatellite instability) status was
evaluated by the PCAWG working group and obtained from the synapse
repository (<https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn8016399>, the data
was downloaded on May 2022). For Hartwig genomes, the MSI status was
downloaded from the supplementary data of Priestley et al., 2019. The
genomes with \>5,000 IDs were labeled as high TMB tumors. The
thresholds were selected based on the minimum number of mutations of
the pre-defined MSI tumors. We then used MSIseq to predict the MSI
status of high TMB tumors.

## Extended sequence context analysis

To analyze a specific signature and indel type of interest, we first
identified the 5 genomes with the highest contribution of the
corresponding signature activity. From these genomes, we extracted all
indels of the relevant type. We then examined the nucleotide sequence
within a 21-base pair window centered on each indel site (±10
nucleotides from the indel position). For each position within this
window, we calculated the frequency of each nucleotide (A, T, C, and
G). The logo was plotted based on the frequency matrix by seqLogo
function of seqLogo R package (version 1.71.0)

\* This is the signature with the best match to the given 89-type
signature.

\*\* indicates that in the linking tumor's spectrum, insertions of
single Ts in long poly-T contexts were set to 0 before calculating
cosine similarity to the 83-type signature.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {#fig-aa}
![](main_figures/cropped/fig1.pdf){width=6.5in}

**The aristolochic acid (AA) indel signatures (signature 23) in the
three classification schemes.**
:::

**(A)** Looking at labeled bars from left to right, at the 83-type
classification highest bar is labeled VTV→VV, indicating a the
deletion of a single T (thymine) surrounded by non-thymines (V, the
preceding V and following V can be different bases, e.g. ATC→AC).
Still in the 83-type classification, the second most frequent deletion
is a deletion of single T from TT flanked by non Ts (VTTV→VTV). In the
89-type classification there is a many-to-many representation of these
(and other mutations) to a peak labeled AT{1,4}→AT{0,3}A, which
indicates 4 possible types of mutations as indicated in the figure
ATA→AA, ATTA→ATA, ATTTA→ATTA, and ATTTTA→ATTTA. To the right are
analogous deletions from e.g. CTA→CA, CTTA→ CTA, etc, and then further
to the right, GTA→GA, GTTA→GTA, etc. Finally, the 476-type
classification makes clear that in fact the main deletions are ATA→AA,
CTA→CA, and GTA→GA.

**(B)** Further to the left in the 83-type classification there are
three light orange bars, with the highest labeled “e.g. TATA→TA, e.g.
TGTG→TG” these bars represent 2-base deletions, with the highest bar
representing the deletion of a 2-base unit from the 2-base unit
duplicated (e.g. a 2-base unit TA, in the duplicated 2-base unit TATA,
with the deletion being TATA→TA). The classification does not capture
information on the bases involved. In the 89-type classification,
these are captured in the tall red bar labeled “many possibilities”,
which represents a wide range of deletions, up to deletions such as
ATATATAT→AT, which are essentially absent in this signature. The
tallest of the corresponding bars in the 476-type classification is
labeled “e.g. TATA→TA, e.g. TGTG→TG”, in one-to-one correspondence
with the light orange bar in the 83-type classification with the
same label. Like the 83-type classification, the 476-classification
does not capture the identity of the bases involved for these
deletions.

**(C)** At the far right, in the 83-type-classification, the light
purple bar indicates 2-base deletions with microhomology, e.g. GAG→G,
where the G flanking the deletion is the microhomologous base. The
bases involved are not captured, and other possibilities include
GTG→G, TAT→T, and many others. In the 89-type classification these and
many other possible deletions are represented by the peak “Many Mh
possibilities”, which includes, in addition, deletions such as
ATCGTA→A, which are essentially absent from this signature. In the
476-type classification, as in the 83-type classification, the highest
bar is labeled “2 base deletions with microhomology”, and it
represents the same set of mutations as the corresponding bar in the
83-type classification. However, in general, even for the 476
classification there is many-to-many mapping of deletions and
insertions of more than 1 base between the 83-type and 476-type
classifications (Table S1).

::: {#fig-assoc}
![](main_figures/cropped/fig4.pdf){height=6.4in}

**Association of indel signatures with cancer types and SBS signatures
and cancer types**
:::

**(A)** Enrichment for presence of 89-type signatures across cancer
types, plus hypermutated (\> 4,000 indels) microsatellite stable (MSS)
tumors and MSI-high (MSI-H) tumors. Only cancer types with odds ratios
\> 6 are shown. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rates based on p
values from Fisher’s exact test of number of tumors with the signature
versus the number without in a given tumor type versus all other
tumors.

**(B)** The heatmap of Spearman correlation coefficients between indel
signatures and various SBS signatures. Signatures were excluded if all
correlation coefficients were between –0.1 and 0.1. Unsupervised
hierarchical clustering of both rows and columns based on signature
proportions identified 8 clusters, boxed and labeled in the figure.
GI: Gastrointestinal.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {#fig-topo}
![](main_figures/cropped/fig5.pdf){height=8.2in}

**83-type mutational signatures asymmetries in strands, replication
timing and DNA regions.**
:::

**(A)** Enrichment of mutations in genic and intergenic regions for
83-type signatures. Each row represents one 83-type signature, where n
reflects the number of cancer types in which the signature was found.
Signatures consistently enriched in genic and intergenic regions with
p values \< 0.05 (Fisher’s exact test) are shown in circles with
yellow and light blue colors, respectively. Grey colors indicate
inconsistent enrichments in different cancer types. Columns display
the odds ratio between the ratio of real mutations and the ratio of
simulated mutations (See Methods). Only odds ratios above 1.10 are
shown. Circle sizes reflect the proportion of cancer types exhibiting
specific enrichment in DNA regions in a signature.

**(B)** Replication strand asymmetries of 83-type signatures. Data are
presented in a format similar to the one in panel (A), with green and
orange colors indicating replication strand asymmetries on the lagging
and leading strands, respectively.

**(C)** Transcription strand asymmetries of 83-type signatures. Data
are presented in a format similar to the one in panel (A), with red
and dark blue colors indicating transcription strand asymmetries on
the transcribed and untranscribed strands, respectively.

**(D)** 83-type signatures associated with early and late replication
timing. Mutation densities of 83-type signatures per decile (y axes)
are presented for early (left) to late (right) replication domains.
Real mutations for signatures are shown as bars, and simulated
mutations are shown as red dashed lines. As shown on top of each plot,
green bars indicate signatures consistently associated with late
replication timing across cancer types (e.g., C_ID3); yellow bars
indicate signatures consistently associated with early replication
timing across cancer types (e.g., C_ID17); purple bars indicate
signatures not affected by replication timing across cancer
types (e.g., ID_K); blue bars indicate signatures showing inconsistent
trend across cancer types (e.g., ID_F).

::: {#fig-rnaseh2}
![](main_figures/cropped/fig6.pdf){height=5.8in}

**Novel signature caused by RNase H2 deficiency and
topoisomerase-1-associated mutagenesis (TOP1-TAM)**
:::

**(A)** The mutational signature of RNase H2 deficiency (InsDel_F in
the 89-type classification, ID_F in the 83-type classification), and a
previously identified mutational signature (InsDel4, C_ID4).

**(B)** Deletions of ≥ 2 bases in the 476-type classification scheme
in InsDel_F compared to InsDel4. InsDel4 has substantial proportions
of deletions of 3 and 4 bases (Del3:U2:R2, Del4:U4:R2, Del3:M2,
Del4:M2, Del4:M3) that are essentially absent in InsDel_F. 
Panel **C** shows Del2:U2:R2 and Del2:M1 examples.

**(C)** Logos of the sequence contexts of 2-base deletions in 5
samples with the highest InsDel_F activity (left) compared to 5
samples with the highest InsDel4 activity (right). The sequence
contexts of the 2-base deletions in InsDel_F are on the whole
different from the contexts of 2-base deletions in InsDel4. In the
lower two sections (DEL:MH:2:1, 2-base deletions with 1 base of
microhomology), the microhomologous bases (T:A) are shaded orange.
